title: Calamari Fritti
subtitle: Italian fried squid rings with lemon
excerpt: Calamari fritti are squid rings dusted lightly in seasoned flour and fried in very hot oil until just crisp. The coating is thin rather than battered. The key is hot oil, small batches, and eating immediately. Served with lemon and nothing else.
sourceNotes: Fried squid is eaten throughout the Mediterranean, but calamari fritti in the Italian style is notable for its very thin flour-only coating rather than a thick batter. The Italian tradition of 'frittura di pesce' (fried seafood) is most associated with the coastal cities of Naples, Genoa, Venice, and Palermo, where mixed fried seafood platters are a staple. The technique of flouring only, without egg or batter, produces a crisper result when the oil temperature is correct.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Slice and dry the squid up to 1 hour ahead. Flour and fry just before serving. Fried calamari does not hold well.
recipe.temperatureNote: Oil temperature: 180°C. Use a thermometer for best results.

content.text: Italian fried squid uses a very light coating of seasoned flour, not a thick batter. The flour crisps in the hot oil and stays thin and delicate, letting the squid flavour come through rather than being buried in bread. The squid cooks in under 2 minutes per batch. The failure modes are cold oil (the squid steams and goes rubbery) and overcrowding (same result). Small batches in very hot oil is the rule.

items.prepNote: cleaned, body cut into 1 cm rings, tentacles left whole

content.text: Pat the squid rings and tentacles dry with kitchen paper. Very dry squid crisps better.
Mix the flour with salt and black pepper in a shallow bowl.
Heat the oil in a deep pan to 180°C. If you do not have a thermometer, drop in a ring of squid: it should sizzle and turn lightly golden within 90 seconds.

Working in batches of no more than a quarter of the squid at a time, toss the rings in the seasoned flour, shake off the excess, and lower carefully into the oil. Fry for 1.5 to 2 minutes until pale gold and crisp. Do not let them turn dark brown.
Lift out with a slotted spoon, drain on kitchen paper, and scatter with sea salt flakes. Eat immediately. Repeat with remaining batches.

items.symptom: The calamari is chewy and tough
items.cause: The squid was cooked for too long, or the oil was not hot enough and the squid stewed instead of frying.
items.fix: Squid toughens after about 2 minutes and then becomes tender again after 20 to 30 minutes. For fried rings, the window is 90 seconds to 2 minutes. Hot oil is essential.

items.symptom: The flour coating is falling off in the oil
items.cause: The squid was wet when it went in the flour.
items.fix: Pat the squid very dry before flouring. Moisture is what stops the coating from adhering.

content.text: Fried squid is eaten from the north to the south of Italy, wherever there is a coast. The Venetian version uses a mixed seafood fry (fritto misto) of squid, prawns, and small fish. In Naples and Palermo it is more commonly served as a standalone dish. The thin flour-only coating is the Italian marker; batter coatings are found elsewhere and produce a very different texture.
